title: How Forward Deployed Engineering is done at Ramp — Leo Mehr

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk's core technical content is about building an agent harness to automate FDE pipeline stages at Ramp — specifically a Notion-based intake agent with multi-round questioning loops, evals with rubrics, and context management. The agent loop architecture, harness design, and the control plane around the model (Slack intake to Notion spec output) are the primary engineering substance. The speaker explicitly frames the FDE lifecycle as a pipeline where 'each stage can be replaced with agents' and discusses harness smoothness and eval infrastructure as future investment areas.

secondary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
secondary.rationale: Evals with rubrics and human feedback are discussed as essential infrastructure for ensuring agent output quality. The speaker identifies evals as a key future investment area alongside the agent harness, though evaluation is not the sole focus of the talk.

secondary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
secondary.rationale: Human-in-the-loop is central to the talk's thesis: FDEs retain responsibility for taste and judgment over final output even as agents automate pipeline stages. The interplay between human scoping discipline and agent automation, and the warning that agents without human judgment produce a 'slop cannon,' are key themes.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: FDE at Ramp is fundamentally about enterprise customer integration workflows, internal engineering operations, and making core product features work for large enterprise customers. The talk's examples (SAP S/4HANA integration, mobile reimbursement for an enterprise customer) are enterprise operations use cases.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: FDE work at Ramp involves API integrations and developer-facing surfaces for enterprise customers. The deployed developer API team is part of the FDE org, and the talk touches on customer-facing API integration as part of scoping decisions.

summary: Leo Mehr, Director of Engineering at Ramp, presents two guiding principles for Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE): "always be scoping" and "scale with tokens." FDE at Ramp sits within the engineering organization—not a go-to-market role—and focuses on making Ramp's core product and agentic features work for large enterprise customers. The org grew from 2 to roughly 30 engineers across deployed, developer API, and AI services teams. The first principle, always be scoping, counters the reflex to say yes to every customer request. Mehr illustrates this with a Friday-night SAP S/4HANA integration ask driven by sales quota rather than genuine customer urgency, and a painful story where two engineers learned iOS and Android to build a mobile reimbursement feature, only to discover the customer mandated iOS-only devices—basic assumptions went unvalidated. The second principle, scale with tokens, asks which stages of the FDE pipeline—context gathering, scoping, spec writing, implementation—can be progressively replaced by agents. Ramp built a Notion-based intake agent that reads requests from an internal Slack channel, conducts multi-round back-and-forth questioning, and auto-generates specs, saving approximately 20% of scoping time and reducing reply latency from hours or days to seconds. The middle pipeline stages remain the hardest to automate. Looking forward, Mehr sees investment in agent harnesses, evals with rubrics and human feedback, and context management. FDEs retain responsibility for taste and judgment over final output. The two principles are interdependent: scoping without token scaling is too slow, but agents without scoping discipline produce a "token-maxing slop cannon." Without both, agent-native competitors will overtake and outcompete you.
whyItMatters: The talk's central thesis is that traditional engineering discipline (scoping) and AI-native automation (token scaling) are not alternatives but interdependent requirements. The software engineering concepts define the organizational structure, pipeline stages, and validation practices that make enterprise engineering work effective. The AI concepts define the automation capabilities—agent harnesses, multi-round questioning, evals, context management—that make that work scalable. The intake-to-spec agent at Ramp is the concrete demonstration of how these concepts interlock: it automates the scoping pipeline stage while embedding scoping discipline (multi-round questioning) into the agent's behavior. Without scoping discipline, agents produce a 'slop cannon' of low-quality output; without token scaling, scoping becomes a bottleneck too slow to serve enterprise customers at scale. The future investment areas—agent harnesses, evals, and context management—represent the engineering challenges of making this interlock reliable in production, and the agent-native competition threat provides the strategic urgency to solve them.
temporalContext: This talk was presented at the AI Engineer conference and published on YouTube on July 28, 2026. Research was conducted as of August 22, 2026. Ramp's FDE organization started in fall 2023 and had grown to approximately 30 engineers by the time of this talk. The Ramp Builders blog post documenting FDE principles was published August 5, 2025. Ramp's $750M raise at $44B valuation was announced around June 2026. The Notion customer case studies were published in May and December 2025. The talk reflects Ramp's FDE practices and agent infrastructure as of mid-2026, a period of rapid maturation in production agent deployments.
takeaways: FDE at Ramp lives in engineering, focused on enterprise customers—not a 'boss mode' go-to-market role

concepts.name: Agent Harness
concepts.explanation: The infrastructure surrounding an LLM that manages agent execution smoothness, context flow between pipeline stages, and output quality. Identified as a key future investment area for FDE teams alongside evals and context management.
concepts.importance: The agent harness is the engineering substrate that makes token-based scaling possible. Without a well-built harness, agents cannot reliably conduct multi-round questioning or produce quality specs.

concepts.name: Multi-Round Questioning Agent
concepts.explanation: An LLM-based agent that conducts iterative back-and-forth questioning with human submitters to gather sufficient context before generating a specification. Evolved from a V1 that asked only a couple of questions to a multi-round version that produces complete specs.
concepts.importance: This is the concrete agent architecture demonstrated in the talk. Its evolution from V1 to multi-round illustrates the iterative refinement process for production agents, and it embodies the interlock between scoping discipline and token scaling.

concepts.name: Evals with Rubrics and Human Feedback
concepts.explanation: Evaluation infrastructure for assessing agent output quality using structured rubrics and human review loops. Identified as essential for ensuring agent-generated specs and pipeline outputs meet quality standards as automation expands.
concepts.importance: Evals are the quality-control mechanism that makes it safe to delegate pipeline stages to agents. Without rubric-based evaluation, there is no systematic way to determine whether an agent's output meets the standard a human FDE would produce.

concepts.name: Context Management for Agents
concepts.explanation: The challenge of capturing tacit product knowledge held by PMs and experienced engineers into agent-accessible form. Notion docs and help articles only provide partial product context, making this a major unsolved challenge for deeper pipeline automation.
concepts.importance: Context management is the key bottleneck preventing automation of the middle pipeline stages. It represents the frontier between what agents can currently do and what still requires human tacit knowledge.

concepts.name: Token-Maxing Slop Cannon
concepts.explanation: The failure mode where agents operate without scoping discipline, producing high-volume but low-quality output. Used as a warning that deploying agents without human judgment guardrails leads to unvalidated, assumption-poor specifications.
concepts.importance: This concept crystallizes the central thesis that agents require scoping discipline to be effective. It is the counterfactual that motivates the interdependency of the two principles.

concepts.name: Agent-Native Competition
concepts.explanation: The competitive threat from organizations built natively around agent-powered engineering pipelines. Teams that fail to adopt both scoping discipline and token scaling will be overtaken by competitors who have integrated agents into their engineering workflow from the ground up.
concepts.importance: Provides the strategic urgency for adopting both principles. It frames agent adoption not as an optimization but as a survival requirement in a market where competitors engineer natively with agents.

concepts.name: Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE)
concepts.explanation: A specialized engineering function that sits within the broader engineering organization, focused on making core product and agentic features work for large enterprise customers. At Ramp, FDE grew from 2 to approximately 30 engineers across deployed, developer API, and AI services teams.
concepts.importance: Defines the organizational context for the entire talk—FDE is the function where both scoping discipline and agent automation principles are applied, and its placement within engineering (not go-to-market) shapes how decisions are made.

concepts.name: Always Be Scoping
concepts.explanation: A principle requiring engineers to pause before accepting customer requests, validating urgency drivers, checking for workarounds, assessing existing API usage, verifying platform assumptions, and considering whether other prospects benefit from the same work before committing to build.
concepts.importance: This is one of the two core principles of the talk. It directly counters the reflex to say yes to every customer request and is illustrated by the SAP S/4HANA Friday-night ask and the mobile reimbursement iOS-only failure story.

concepts.name: FDE Pipeline Stages
concepts.explanation: The engineering lifecycle—context gathering, scoping, spec writing, implementation—viewed as a pipeline where each stage can be progressively automated or replaced by agents. The middle stages (well-shaped spec to working product) remain the hardest to automate.
concepts.importance: Provides the structural framework for the 'scale with tokens' principle. It is the lens through which teams identify which engineering work can be delegated to agents versus requiring human judgment.

concepts.name: Intake-to-Spec Automation
concepts.explanation: An automated workflow where a Notion-based agent reads unstructured requests from an internal Slack channel, conducts multi-round back-and-forth questioning with submitters, and generates structured specifications, replacing manual scoping. Saved approximately 20% of scoping time and cut reply latency from hours/days to seconds.
concepts.importance: This is the concrete production implementation that demonstrates both principles working together: the agent embeds scoping discipline (multi-round questioning) while automating the pipeline stage (spec generation).

concepts.name: Scoping Validation Checklist
concepts.explanation: The systematic set of questions an FDE should ask before building: What is driving the urgency? Are there workarounds? Can the customer use existing APIs? Do other prospects benefit? What platform assumptions are being made? Failure to apply this checklist led to wasted Android development in the mobile reimbursement story.
concepts.importance: Operationalizes the 'always be scoping' principle into concrete steps, and serves as the guardrail that prevents agents from producing unvalidated output.

sections.title: Introduction: FDE principles at Ramp
sections.summary: Mehr introduces himself as Director of Engineering at Ramp, where FDE grew from 2 to ~30 engineers. FDE lives within engineering and focuses on making core product and agentic features work for enterprise customers. He announces two guiding principles: always be scoping and scale with tokens.

sections.title: Principle one: always be scoping
sections.summary: The reflex to say yes to every customer request is wrong. FDEs must help customers succeed but deliver the right software, not endlessly say yes. Scoping means gathering context about what actually matters before building.

sections.title: The Friday night SAP integration ask
sections.summary: An enterprise sales rep demands an SAP S/4HANA integration on Friday night for a strategic logo. A well-trained FDE pauses to ask what drives the urgency, whether workarounds exist, whether the customer can hit Ramp's API, and whether other prospects benefit from the same work.

sections.title: When scoping goes wrong: the mobile reimbursement story
sections.summary: Two FDEs learned iOS and Android to build a mobile reimbursement feature for an enterprise customer, only to discover the customer mandated iOS-only devices. Basic assumptions went unvalidated, wasting weeks of effort and underscoring the cost of skipping scoping.

sections.title: Using agents for the FDE pipeline
sections.summary: Scoping mastery alone is insufficient; FDEs must scale with model capabilities. Mehr frames the FDE lifecycle—context gathering, scoping, spec writing, implementation—as a pipeline where each stage can be progressively replaced by agents.

sections.title: Automating request intake into specs
sections.summary: Requests arrive via an internal Slack channel with high variance in detail. Previously FDEs manually read, understood, and scoped each request. Ramp wired this step to a Notion agent that conducts back-and-forth questioning with submitters until a spec is ready.

sections.title: Building the spec agent in Notion
sections.summary: V1 of the Notion agent simply took the request and asked a couple of questions. After iteration it now does multiple rounds of questioning before creating a spec. A penguin mascot makes it approachable. Mehr estimates ~20% time savings on scoping and latency cut to seconds.

sections.title: The agent harness and evals
sections.summary: Future FDE work centers on agent harness smoothness, output quality via evals with rubrics and human feedback, and context management—capturing tacit PM knowledge into agents. FDEs retain responsibility for taste and judgment over final output. The middle pipeline stages remain the hardest to automate.

sections.title: The future of FDE needs both
sections.summary: Scoping without token scaling is too slow. But agents without scoping discipline produce a 'token maxing slop cannon.' Mehr warns that without both principles, agent-native competitors will overtake and outcompete you. The future of FDE requires both always be scoping and scaling with tokens.

organization.name: Ramp
organization.summary: Ramp is an all-in-one spend management platform founded in March 2019 and headquartered in New York, NY. It combines corporate cards, expense management, accounts payable, travel, procurement, accounting automation, and banking into a single platform, serving 70,000+ businesses. Ramp has integrated AI agents across its platform, including a Policy Agent for automated expense review and multiple AP agents for invoice processing, fraud prevention, approval routing, and payment. The company's Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team, led by Director of Engineering Leo Mehr, embeds engineers with enterprise customers to deliver customized implementations, build generalized platform features, and develop AI tooling to scale customer onboarding. The FDE org grew from 2 to approximately 30 engineers across deployed, developer API, and AI services teams. Ramp is valued at approximately $44B and has raised over $3.7B in total funding from investors including Founders Fund, Thrive Capital, Sequoia, and Stripe.

technologies.label: Notion AI Agent Platform
technologies.summary: Ramp uses Notion's AI Agent platform as the primary surface for building and deploying internal AI agents. The flagship implementation is an intake-to-spec agent that reads customer requests from an internal Slack channel, conducts multi-round back-and-forth questioning with submitters, and auto-generates structured specifications. The agent evolved from a V1 that asked only a couple of questions to a multi-round version with a penguin mascot. Ramp runs 300+ Notion Agents in production. The intake agent saved approximately 20% of scoping time and reduced reply latency from hours or days to seconds.
technologies.role: Primary demonstrated technology—the Notion-based intake-to-spec agent is the centerpiece example of how Ramp applies both FDE principles in production, with quantified impact of ~20% time savings and latency reduction to seconds

technologies.label: FDE Agent Pipeline Architecture
technologies.summary: The architectural concept of decomposing the Forward Deployed Engineering lifecycle into discrete pipeline stages—context gathering, scoping, spec writing, implementation—where each stage can be progressively replaced by agents. The intake and early scoping stages have been automated at Ramp via the Notion-based agent; the middle stages (well-shaped spec to working product) remain the hardest to automate due to the challenge of capturing tacit product knowledge into agent-accessible context.
technologies.role: Conceptual framework that structures the entire 'scale with tokens' principle; the speaker explicitly frames each FDE lifecycle stage as replaceable by agents and identifies which stages have been automated and which remain manual

technologies.label: Agent Evaluation with Rubrics and Human Feedback
technologies.primary: Evaluation with Rubrics and Human Feedback
technologies.summary: Structured evaluation infrastructure using rubrics and human review loops to systematically assess agent output quality. Identified as a key future investment area for FDE teams alongside agent harness smoothness and context management. Evals ensure that agent-generated specifications and pipeline outputs meet the quality standards a human FDE would produce, making it safe to progressively delegate pipeline stages to agents. Humans retain responsibility for taste and judgment over final output.
technologies.role: Identified as a key future investment area for ensuring agent output quality as automation expands across pipeline stages; paired with the principle that humans retain responsibility for taste and judgment over final output

technologies.label: Agent Harness
technologies.summary: The infrastructure surrounding LLMs that manages agent execution smoothness, context flow between pipeline stages, and overall output quality. Identified as a key future investment area for FDE teams alongside evals and context management. The harness is the engineering substrate that makes token-based scaling reliable in production—without a well-built harness, agents cannot reliably conduct multi-round questioning or produce quality specs. Context management, capturing tacit PM knowledge into agent-accessible form, is the key unsolved challenge within the harness.
technologies.role: Identified as a key future investment area; the engineering substrate that makes token-based scaling possible and reliable in production
